fixes.explanation: That's it, friend. Job remembers God's lamp shining above his head, and he says he walked through the darkness by His light. I think that's a big part of what he misses. No flashlight on earth competes with that.
That's not the lamp Job names, friend. He says it was God's lamp that shone above his head, and he walked through the darkness by His light. I bet that made the dark feel a lot smaller.

True, baker. Job says "…my steps were bathed in cream and the rock poured out for me streams of oil!" (Job 29:6) That's a man walking through plenty. I've only ever been bathed in cookie crumbs, and I'm not complaining.
Right, baker. Job says the young men saw him and withdrew. That's how they responded when he went out to the city gate and took his seat in the public square.
Bowing to the ground is a big move, but Job doesn't say it. He says the young men saw him and withdrew. They pulled back, and that's all the verse tells us.
Friend, Job says the opposite. He says the young men saw him and withdrew, and withdrawing means pulling back. I'd be the one running up for a hug, but that's just me.
Not quite, friend. Job says the old men rose to their feet. The text tells us they stood up, so this one is False. I think that says a lot about how they saw him.
That's the reason. Job says people called him blessed because he rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had no helper. Notice what he names there. It's the people he rescued.

I understand the guess, but Job never mentions a house here. He says those who heard him called him blessed because he rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had no helper. A house isn't in that verse.
False is right. Job says the dying man blessed him, and he made the widow's heart sing for joy. Those are the people he's remembering. I think it's a tender thing to recall.

Followed sounds nice, but Job picks a different word. He says, "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; justice was my robe and my turban." (Job 29:14) It's something he put on, from robe to turban. Righteousness wasn't tagging along behind him, it was what he wore.
Feet, yes. Job says he served as eyes to the blind and as feet to the lame. Those are his words for how he served them. That's a man you want at your side.
Hands is a good guess, and trust me, I know the value of good hands. Mine are a mustache. But Job says he served as feet to the lame, right after saying he was eyes to the blind.
Ears fit a man people came to for counsel. But for the lame, Job says he served as feet. Right before that, he says he was eyes to the blind.

King it is. Job says, "So I dwelt as a king among his troops, as a comforter of the mourners." (Job 29:25) And look at how he finishes that line. Right after the king comparison, he says he dwelt as a comforter of the mourners.
Camels are a fair guess, but Job names another animal. He says he would have refused to put their fathers with his sheep dogs. Those are his words, not mine.

Job doesn't mention thieves, friend. He says, "…God has unstrung my bow and afflicted me…" (Job 30:11) and he names God as the one who unstrung it. He describes the bow as unstrung. That's a big change from the way he spoke of it before.

I see why you'd say friends, since Job talks a lot about people pulling away. But in this verse, Job says the terrors drive away his dignity as by the wind. He also says his prosperity has passed like a cloud. Friends aren't named there.

Servants are a fair guess, but Job doesn't name them here. He says terrors are turned loose against him, and they drive away his dignity as by the wind. His prosperity, he says, has passed like a cloud.

That's not what Job says. He asks, "Have I not wept for those in trouble? Has my soul not grieved for the needy?" (Job 30:25) He describes weeping and grieving for people in need. Staying away isn't the picture.
Mourning. Job says, "My harp is tuned to mourning and my flute to the sound of weeping." (Job 30:31) His harp and his flute are tuned to grief. I think it's a sad note to end a speech on.

Victory is a hopeful guess, friend, but Job doesn't say that. He says, "My harp is tuned to mourning and my flute to the sound of weeping." (Job 30:31) The music he describes is mourning and weeping. That's how this speech ends.
